A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work and retain the TCV definition and Theorem 3.4. Their text, equations, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite the substantial revision.

before.justification: v1 reports original Gaussian-mixture autoencoding and MNIST experiments, including spectral evolution, centroid-based training comparisons, and architectural sensitivity studies in Figures 1–5.

after.justification: v2 reports original Gaussian-mixture and MNIST experiments, including repeated-initialization studies and appendix results on residual networks and feature collapse in Figures 1–7.

M1.justification: The original feedforward formulation remains, but v2 introduces separately weighted first-layer decay and feature-norm regularization in its experimental objective (Section 5.2). It also adds residual-layer updates and the corresponding representation-cost formulation in Appendix C.

E1.justification: Gaussian-mixture and MNIST data remain, but the reported synthetic task changes from autoencoding in v1 Sections 6.1–6.2 to one-hot classification in v2 Section 5.1. The deep-linear autoencoding study disappears; the additional MNIST experiments retain classification coverage.

E2.justification: v1 Section 6.2 and Figure 2 explicitly compare full-data training with centroid-based training. v2 removes this paired comparison with the deep-linear study. Neither version provides an extensive comparison against external baseline algorithms.

E3.justification: v2 introduces MNIST experiments using 200 examples, width-200 networks, and five-, ten-, fifteen-layer and residual configurations. Section 5.2 specifies training beyond interpolation to data loss below 10^-6, while Section 5.3 measures numerical rank at 10^-5 relative error. These differ from v1's protocols, including architectural sweeps using 10% rank tolerance.

E4.justification: v1's full-versus-centroid analysis and systematic width/depth sweeps are removed. v2 adds first-layer-regularization sensitivity, observed-versus-predicted spectra, initialization robustness, residual-weight decay analyses, and Gram-matrix and projected-feature case studies (Sections 5.2–5.3 and Appendix D).

E5.justification: v1 does not report repeated-run counts or uncertainty bands. v2 Section 5.3 and Figure 3 introduce a study with 100 random unitary initializations, reporting averages and minimum-to-maximum shading for TCV, loss, and numerical rank. This is new replication and variability reporting.

E6.justification: v1's centroid-distance curves and MNIST spectral-tail and architectural-sweep results are removed. v2 reports spectral agreement as first-layer regularization decreases, TCV convergence and ranks near ten across initializations, residual-weight shrinkage, and emerging class structure (Figures 2–7). These are new or replaced findings under different settings.

T1.justification: Theorem 3.4 and its supporting argument are retained, but v1's Gaussian concentration result and linear-case Theorems 5.3–5.4 are removed. v2 adds DNC1 definitions, representation-cost constraints, global-optimality, reachability and stability theorems, residual-network theory, and a Gram-matrix characterization, with extensive new appendix proofs.

C1.justification: v1 principally claims that clustered representations and weight decay imply approximate low rank. v2 additionally claims global optimality of DNC1 configurations, essentially barrier-free reachability, stability under first-layer regularization, and prediction of final singular-value structure. These substantially broaden the abstract, introduction, and conclusion.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the new landscape results as explaining the universality and late-training emergence of collapse. It adds substantive discussion of representability, spectral and rank constraints, width requirements, first-layer regularization, and large-depth limits, including the qualification that accumulation points are not automatically guaranteed.

D1.justification: v2 adds NVIDIA A100 80GB hardware information and explicit MNIST sample counts, widths, regularization coefficients, convergence targets, and the meaning of plotted optimization steps. Conversely, the revised Gaussian experiment omits v1's explicit sample count, input dimension, hidden widths, and gradient-descent stopping description.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around neural-collapse optimality and representation costs, including works by Jacot and Súkeník and collaborators. It removes several references supporting v1's linear-case analysis and its language-model rank-reduction motivation. The relationship to prior research changes beyond bibliographic updates.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion are substantially rewritten around deep neural collapse. The Gaussian and linear special-case organization is replaced by a global-optimality narrative and appendices A–D. The retained proof of Theorem 3.4 moves from the main text to Appendix A.3.

P2.justification: The body changes from two-column to single-column layout. Figure 1 changes from a 2-by-2 heatmap arrangement to a single row with different color encoding and a TCV axis label. Other figures are replaced or added, including spectral overlays, shaded convergence plots, and full-page appendix visualization grids.

improvement.justification: v2 adds useful repeated-run evidence, but its central advance over v1's conditional bound includes an invalid all-minimizers claim. Under Theorem 4.2, take two layers, X=I4, two balanced one-hot classes, cubing activations, and C=1: Z1=sqrt(2)I4 satisfies the constraints and attains minimum representation cost 1, yet has within-class variation 1. Appendix B incorrectly forces trailing singular values to zero. This undermines the new global-optimality and representation-structure claims, outweighing the experimental and reporting gains.
